questions.article: A Message for the New Year
questions.q: On what two-point formula, the writer says, is Islamic spirituality based?
options: Travel and study
Not quite. The article says: Simple living and high thinking.
Simple living and high thinking
Yes. “Nothing mysterious in nature.”
Wealth and generosity
Not quite. The article says: Simple living and high thinking.
Long retreats and silence
Not quite. The article says: Simple living and high thinking.
questions.rationale: “Islamic spirituality is based on a two point formula: Simple Living and High Thinking.”

questions.article: 125 Years of Swami Vivekananda in the West
questions.q: What formula of Swami Vivekananda does the editorial commend for living amid many religions?
options: “Follow All, Question None”
Not quite. The article says: “Follow One, Hate None”.
“Follow One, Hate None”
Right. Follow one religion and respect all.
“Follow the Majority”
Not quite. The article says: “Follow One, Hate None”.
“Follow None, Study All”
Not quite. The article says: “Follow One, Hate None”.
questions.rationale: “His formula was, ‘Follow One, Hate None’… this is the simplest and most natural formula—to follow one religion, and respect all.”

questions.article: 125 Years of Swami Vivekananda in the West
questions.q: The editorial says differences among people “are not evil.” What reason does it give?
options: They keep communities apart and safe
Not quite. The article says: They create challenges, and challenges lead to development and progress.
They exist only in appearance
Not quite. The article says: They create challenges, and challenges lead to development and progress.
They create challenges, and challenges lead to development and progress
Well read. So they are to be accepted, not removed.
They will disappear in time
Not quite. The article says: They create challenges, and challenges lead to development and progress.
questions.rationale: “But differences are not evil; they are a blessing as they create challenges, which lead to development and progress in the world.”

questions.q: Asked what fanaticism was, how did the Prophet define it?
options: “That you love your people”
Not quite. The article says: “That you help your people in wrongdoing”.
“That you worship too much”
Not quite. The article says: “That you help your people in wrongdoing”.
“That you help your people in wrongdoing”
Yes. Loyalty must not override justice.
“That you speak your mind”
Not quite. The article says: “That you help your people in wrongdoing”.
questions.rationale: “Someone asked the Prophet, ‘What fanaticism was?’ and he replied: ‘That you help your people in wrongdoing’.”

questions.q: A man asked three times how often he should forgive his servant. What was the Prophet’s answer?
options: “Only if he asks”
Not quite. The article says: “Seventy times every day”.
“Three times in all”
Not quite. The article says: “Seventy times every day”.
“Once, and then warn him”
Not quite. The article says: “Seventy times every day”.
“Seventy times every day”
Correct. Forgiveness without keeping count.
questions.rationale: “‘Forgive your servant seventy times everyday’, said the Prophet.”

questions.q: Abdullah ibn Abbas left his retreat in the mosque to speak to a troubled man’s creditor. What reason did he give?
options: His retreat had already ended
Not quite. The article says: The Prophet had said that hastening to help a brother is better than twenty years in retreat.
The Prophet had said that hastening to help a brother is better than twenty years in retreat
Right. Service came before seclusion.
He wished to leave the mosque
Not quite. The article says: The Prophet had said that hastening to help a brother is better than twenty years in retreat.
The creditor was his relative
Not quite. The article says: The Prophet had said that hastening to help a brother is better than twenty years in retreat.
questions.rationale: “I have heard the Prophet say that running to the assistance of one’s brother and doing one’s utmost to help him is better than remaining twenty years in retreat.”

questions.q: The Prophet found a seller’s heap of grain wet underneath. What did he tell him?
options: To dry it before selling
Not quite. The article says: To put the wet grain on top where buyers could see it – those who deceive “do not belong with us”.
To put the wet grain on top where buyers could see it – those who deceive “do not belong with us”
Yes. Honest trade hides no defect.
To lower the price of the whole heap
Not quite. The article says: To put the wet grain on top where buyers could see it – those who deceive “do not belong with us”.
To stop selling grain
Not quite. The article says: To put the wet grain on top where buyers could see it – those who deceive “do not belong with us”.
questions.rationale: “Then why not put the wet portion on top, so that people can see it… Those who deceive others do not belong with us.”

questions.q: Hoyle and Wickramasinghe each calculated the odds of life arising by chance. To what conclusion did the figures drive them?
options: That earlier scientists had been right
Not quite. The article says: That life could not have begun accidentally; its conditions point to deliberate creation.
That life could not have begun accidentally; its conditions point to deliberate creation
Well reasoned. Against their own earlier assumptions.
That life is common throughout the universe
Not quite. The article says: That life could not have begun accidentally; its conditions point to deliberate creation.
That the question cannot be studied
Not quite. The article says: That life could not have begun accidentally; its conditions point to deliberate creation.
questions.rationale: “Once we saw that the probability of life originating at random is so utterly miniscule as to make it absurd, it became sensible to think that the properties of physics on which life depends are in every respect deliberate.”

questions.q: Whenever people work together, grievances arise. What does the article say each person must become?
options: A spokesman for his own rights
Not quite. The article says: A “self-correcting machine” – defusing resentment within himself.
A judge of his colleagues
Not quite. The article says: A “self-correcting machine” – defusing resentment within himself.
A careful record-keeper of wrongs
Not quite. The article says: A “self-correcting machine” – defusing resentment within himself.
A “self-correcting machine” – defusing resentment within himself
Exactly. As Khalid did when removed from command.
questions.rationale: “Every individual has to turn himself into a self-correcting machine. He must defuse within himself the antipathy which he feels towards another.”

questions.q: The verses speak of things “casting their shadows right and left, prostrating themselves before God.” What lesson does the commentary read in a shadow?
options: Shadows show the time for prayer
Not quite. The article says: Falling flat on the ground, it symbolises the humility with which man should bow before his Creator.
Falling flat on the ground, it symbolises the humility with which man should bow before his Creator
Well read. Everything around teaches obedience.
Shadows prove the sun moves
Not quite. The article says: Falling flat on the ground, it symbolises the humility with which man should bow before his Creator.
Shadows are a sign of weakness
Not quite. The article says: Falling flat on the ground, it symbolises the humility with which man should bow before his Creator.
questions.rationale: “The shadow of a thing standing erect falls on the ground. In this way, it symbolizes kneeling down (sajdah). It shows symbolically how a man should bow down before his Creator.”
